articles.title: SQLite WAL Mode Can Lock Short-Lived Readers
articles.summary: SQLite's Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode can lock short-lived readers, causing rare but constant database is locked errors in extremely rarely written-to databases. The issue arises from the connection lifecycle of WAL mode, which requires exclusive locks when opening or closing an empty database, potentially leading to brief exclusive access for new readers during those windows. This problem becomes more apparent with read-only connections that are opened and closed independently without connection pooling, resulting in a surprising amount of write churn even on effectively read-only systems.

articles.title: Maybe we should revisit microkernels
articles.summary: Microkernels offer better security, reliability, and modularity compared to mainstream operating systems. A microkernel system provides a bug in one driver only gives an attacker access to that subsystem, whereas in mainstream OS systems, unlimited access can be gained by exploiting vulnerabilities throughout the entire system. This is due to the lack of direct hardware access for userspace processes, resulting in frequent context switches and increased overhead. The introduction of I/O Multiprocessor Units (IOMMUs) has enabled virtually eliminating context switches from the happy path, reducing latency while maintaining zero-overhead IPC capabilities.

articles.title: Memory Safety Absolutists
articles.summary: Rust developers who claim to care about memory safety may genuinely be concerned with making software safer, not just criticizing languages that compete with Rust. The article notes that most memory safety related discourse has been relatively simple in the past, but now a new way to make C and C++ code memory safe is being developed using Fil-C, which combines GC and InvisiCaps to track memory accessible by a pointer. This approach aims to minimize memory safety vulnerabilities and may be more effective than traditional methods, such as RAII or smart pointers. However, the article suggests that this new technology may not be enough to convince Rust developers who claim to care about memory safety, and instead may be seen as disingenuous.
